codebook.source: MONK-2 problem (Thrun et al. 1991), PMLB 'monk2' deduplicated to the 432 input configurations; attributes a1-a6 are abstract (no real-world meaning), so statements are phrased in rule terms on the attribute values

ann_25.text: Through this part, which reads a2, a3 and a6, changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' for the typical case with a3 = 2, from about 3% to about 5%, while with a3 = 1 it stays below 1%.

ann_26.text: This part of the model acts on 290 of the 345 training cases, and 85 of them are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 1, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 2, a6 = 1), it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 98% without the part to below 1% with it.
For the typical case with a5 other than 1, changing a1 from 1 to 3 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 9% to about 93%, while with a5 = 1 it stays below 1%.

Through this part, for the typical case it acts on, giving a4 its first value slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes', and moving a5 away from its first value slightly lowers it, staying below 1%.
Moving a1 away from its first value slightly lowers it as well (on the training data only).
The effect of a1 also depends slightly on a3, a4 and a6, with the typical case staying at about 3% or below.

ann_27.text: Through this part, moving a5 from 1 to 4 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 49%, while moving it to 2 or 3 raises it only to about 9% (on the training data only).
Moving a1 away from its first value slightly raises it, staying below 1%.
Moving a3 or a6 away from its first value, or changing a2 from 3 to 2, also slightly raises it, and giving a2 or a4 its first value slightly lowers it (on the training data only).

ann_25.original: Pair gate over a2=1, a3=1, a6=1. P = ReLU(0.628 + 2.96 z(a2:1) - 2.11 z(a2:3) + 3.11 z(a3:1) - 4.21 z(a6:2)) = ReLU(-7.469 + 6.26[a2=1] + 6.22[a3=1] + 8.42[a6=1] - 4.44[a2=3]). Evidence (closed form; exhaustive enumeration of the 12 (a2,a3,a6) patterns): all three indicators -> 13.43; two -> 7.22 (a2,a6), 7.17 (a3,a6), 5.01 (a2,a3), 2.73 (a3,a6 with a2=3); one -> 0 except a6=1 alone with a2=2 -> 0.95; none -> 0. So P is a graded at-least-two-of-three counter over the indicators of a2, a3, a6. Train sensitivity is largest for a6:2 (2.17), then a3:1 (1.60), a2:1 (1.53), a2:3 (1.09). It supplies count information for a2 and a6, which the direct linear path barely weighs.
ann_25.proposed: A small part through which a2 = 2 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' when a3 = 2.

ann_26.original: Serial composition: pair gate P feeds the low-count gate L (node 584); outputs (P, L). L = ReLU(1.308 + 5.043[a1=2] + 5.853[a1=3] - 1.583[a3=1] - 5.530[a4=1] - 5.532[a5=1] - 0.603[a6=1] - 1.885 P) ~= ReLU(6.7 - 5.4[a1=1] - 5.53[a4=1] - 5.53[a5=1] - 1.58[a3=1] - 0.60[a6=1] - 1.885 P). L is a 'too few indicators' detector: large (up to 7.16) when none of a1=1, a4=1, a5=1 hold and P is quiet; closed by a first value of a1/a4/a5 plus any further indicator, or by P (the P -> L inhibition routes a2/a3/a6 count evidence into the lower edge). Evidence: over all 432 inputs, L>0 for 100% of inputs with 0 or 1 first values (means 6.76, 4.04), 30% with exactly 2 (mean 0.22; L stays ~1.2-1.3 for pairs {a1,a2}, {a2,a4}, {a2,a5}), 0% with >=3. Train sensitivity of L: a1:3 0.96, a4:1 0.90, a5:1 0.85, a1:2 0.84, a3:1 0.28, others <=0.23. Local train ablation: P=0 everywhere -> acc 0.672 / AUC 0.614; L removed -> 0.667 / 0.632 (full 0.855 / 0.946).
ann_26.proposed: This part acts on 290 training cases and pushes their predicted probability of 'yes' down (from about 98% to below 1% for the typical one); with it, changing a1 from 1 to 3 turns the typical case with a5 other than 1 to 'yes'.

ann_27.original: Decreasing weighted linear count ramp (direct input->output connections). Per attribute value: a1: =1 -2.97, =2 +1.27, =3 +2.01; a2: =1 -0.74, =2 +1.17, =3 -0.38; a3: =1 -2.66, =2 +2.80; a4: =1 -5.52, =2/3 +2.48; a5: =1 -7.42, =2/3 +1.74, =4 +4.03; a6: =1 -0.27, =2 +0.29. Each first-value indicator lowers the sum by an unequal amount: a5 (9.2-11.4) and a4 (8.0) count heavily, a3 (5.5) and a1 (4.2-5.0) moderately, a2 (0.4-1.9) and a6 (0.56) barely. Evidence (closed form; enumeration of 432 inputs): ramp + output bias averages 12.3, 8.1, 3.6, -1.1, -6.2, -11.6, -17.3 for 0..6 first values (range -17.3 to 15.0). It is the upper edge of the response peak. Alone (with bias) it gives train accuracy 0.565, AUC 0.602.
ann_27.proposed: A linear score through which a5 away from its first value raises the predicted probability of 'yes', much more for a5 = 4 than for a5 = 2 or 3 (on the training data only), with small effects of the other attributes.

summary.text: The typical case has the most common value of each attribute (a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1); with a5 other than 1 instead, changing a1 from 1 to 3 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 9% to about 93%, while with a5 = 1 it stays below 1%.
One part of the model acts on 290 of the 345 training cases, and 85 of them are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case this part acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 1, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 2, a6 = 1), it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 98% without the part to below 1% with it.

Through another part, moving a5 from 1 to 4 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 49%, while moving it to 2 or 3 raises it only to about 9% (on the training data only).

parts.name: weighted_count_peak
parts.original_hypothesis: Root: score = sigmoid(2.236 + Ramp - 0.918 P - 5.804 L). Ramp falls with weighted indicator count (upper edge); L subtracts up to 41.6 when there are 0-1 indicators (lower edge); P adds an extra penalty (0.918 x 0.95..13.4) when >=2 of a2/a3/a6 are first values and, through L, closes the lower edge. Unconnected inputs a4:2, a4:3, a5:2, a5:3 (no enabled edges) have zero effect; a4 and a5 are read only through a4:1, a5:1, a5:4. Evidence: mean output pre-activation by number of first values (432 inputs): -26.9, -15.4, +0.55, -5.4, -13.2, -21.3, -29.7 for 0..6, a peak at two. Positive predictions: 0/24, 9/92 (8 of them a1=1 alone), 87/142, 4/113, 0/61. The peak is imperfect because the indicators are weighted unequally: a4=1 and a5=1 each count almost double, so pairs containing a5 and {a2,a4},{a4,a5} mostly score negative, while a1=1 alone often scores positive. Train (n=345): accuracy 0.855, AUC 0.946; agreement with the MONK-2 rule on all 432 inputs 0.843. Train sensitivity of output: L 0.31, Ramp 0.053, P 0.049.

parts.name: count_stage
parts.original_hypothesis: Serial composition: pair gate P feeds the low-count gate L (node 584); outputs (P, L). L = ReLU(1.308 + 5.043[a1=2] + 5.853[a1=3] - 1.583[a3=1] - 5.530[a4=1] - 5.532[a5=1] - 0.603[a6=1] - 1.885 P) ~= ReLU(6.7 - 5.4[a1=1] - 5.53[a4=1] - 5.53[a5=1] - 1.58[a3=1] - 0.60[a6=1] - 1.885 P). L is a 'too few indicators' detector: large (up to 7.16) when none of a1=1, a4=1, a5=1 hold and P is quiet; closed by a first value of a1/a4/a5 plus any further indicator, or by P (the P -> L inhibition routes a2/a3/a6 count evidence into the lower edge). Evidence: over all 432 inputs, L>0 for 100% of inputs with 0 or 1 first values (means 6.76, 4.04), 30% with exactly 2 (mean 0.22; L stays ~1.2-1.3 for pairs {a1,a2}, {a2,a4}, {a2,a5}), 0% with >=3. Train sensitivity of L: a1:3 0.96, a4:1 0.90, a5:1 0.85, a1:2 0.84, a3:1 0.28, others <=0.23. Local train ablation: P=0 everywhere -> acc 0.672 / AUC 0.614; L removed -> 0.667 / 0.632 (full 0.855 / 0.946).

parts.name: pair_gate_a2a3a6
parts.original_hypothesis: Pair gate over a2=1, a3=1, a6=1. P = ReLU(0.628 + 2.96 z(a2:1) - 2.11 z(a2:3) + 3.11 z(a3:1) - 4.21 z(a6:2)) = ReLU(-7.469 + 6.26[a2=1] + 6.22[a3=1] + 8.42[a6=1] - 4.44[a2=3]). Evidence (closed form; exhaustive enumeration of the 12 (a2,a3,a6) patterns): all three indicators -> 13.43; two -> 7.22 (a2,a6), 7.17 (a3,a6), 5.01 (a2,a3), 2.73 (a3,a6 with a2=3); one -> 0 except a6=1 alone with a2=2 -> 0.95; none -> 0. So P is a graded at-least-two-of-three counter over the indicators of a2, a3, a6. Train sensitivity is largest for a6:2 (2.17), then a3:1 (1.60), a2:1 (1.53), a2:3 (1.09). It supplies count information for a2 and a6, which the direct linear path barely weighs.

parts.name: linear_count_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: Decreasing weighted linear count ramp (direct input->output connections). Per attribute value: a1: =1 -2.97, =2 +1.27, =3 +2.01; a2: =1 -0.74, =2 +1.17, =3 -0.38; a3: =1 -2.66, =2 +2.80; a4: =1 -5.52, =2/3 +2.48; a5: =1 -7.42, =2/3 +1.74, =4 +4.03; a6: =1 -0.27, =2 +0.29. Each first-value indicator lowers the sum by an unequal amount: a5 (9.2-11.4) and a4 (8.0) count heavily, a3 (5.5) and a1 (4.2-5.0) moderately, a2 (0.4-1.9) and a6 (0.56) barely. Evidence (closed form; enumeration of 432 inputs): ramp + output bias averages 12.3, 8.1, 3.6, -1.1, -6.2, -11.6, -17.3 for 0..6 first values (range -17.3 to 15.0). It is the upper edge of the response peak. Alone (with bias) it gives train accuracy 0.565, AUC 0.602.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
